summary: Build with a model as one part of the system: contain it, test it, and know what it costs.

items.text: The model proposes, and the code decides. Numbers, rules, and permissions live in code.
Put the model behind a port that the core owns. Each provider is an adapter, with a fake for tests.
Validate each output with a schema and business checks. Repair once, then hand off to a person.
Use a fixed workflow when you can list the steps. Use an agent only when the steps depend on the input.
Code owns the state. Each state has its own tools, exit conditions, and deterministic guards.
Keep the internal decision and the reply apart. Internal labels never reach the user.
Grade with code checks first: schema, labels, tool calls, final state, forbidden content.
An LLM judge uses a binary rubric, and you calibrate it against expert labels before you trust it.
Cost of one call = (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price) ÷ 1,000,000. State each price as an assumption.
For English, assume about 4/3 tokens for each word and 150 spoken words each minute. A 30-minute call is about 6,000 tokens.
Compare cost per task with value per task. Count the review time of people: it often costs more than the model.
Process once, use many times: extract the facts of each item once, store them as rows, and build each report from the rows.
Total time = time to first token + output tokens ÷ output speed. A long output is the usual cause of a slow call.
Start from when the person acts. Choose the cheapest processing that is ready before that moment.
Voice: aim for less than about 1 second from the end of speech to the first audio. The model is only about a third of it.
Voice cost per minute = telephony + speech to text + model + text to speech + hosting.
